legend: Despite being best girl, Kirisu-sensei still is terrible at math. She has combined the concepts of greatest common factor and least common multiple together!

The greatest common multiple of two numbers a$$$a$$$ and b$$$b$$$ (gcm) is the largest number that both a$$$a$$$ and b$$$b$$$ can divide. Since this number is very large (in fact it's infinite), you are asked to find it mod some number c$$$c$$$. In this context, largest under mod means the maximum value of (d mod c)$$$(d \text{ mod } c)$$$ over any d$$$d$$$ that both a$$$a$$$ and b$$$b$$$ divide d$$$d$$$.
x=max$$x = \max_{a \mid d, b \mid d}(d \text{ mod } c)$$
output x$$$x$$$ as defined above (a \mid d$$$a \mid d$$$ means that a$$$a$$$ divides d$$$d$$$).
input: The first line contains one integer T$$$T$$$, the number of testcases (1 \leq T \leq 3366)$$$(1 \leq T \leq 3366)$$$.

The following T$$$T$$$ lines each contain three integers a, b, c$$$a, b, c$$$, where a$$$a$$$ and b$$$b$$$ are the two numbers to find the gcm of and c$$$c$$$ is the mod (1 \leq a, b  \lt  c \leq 10^9)$$$(1 \leq a, b  \lt  c \leq 10^9)$$$.
output: For each testcase, output \text{gcm}(a, b) \mod c$$$\text{gcm}(a, b) \mod c$$$ or \max_{a \mid d, b \mid d}(d \text{ mod } c)$$$\max_{a \mid d, b \mid d}(d \text{ mod } c)$$$.
note: If we pick d = 18$$$d = 18$$$ on the first sample, we would output x = 18 \text{ mod } 10$$$x = 18 \text{ mod } 10$$$. It is impossible to have a better answer. Note that d = 48$$$d = 48$$$ or d = 888888$$$d = 888888$$$ also give a maximal x = 8$$$x = 8$$$.
In the second sample, picking d = 189$$$d = 189$$$ gives a maximal x = 9$$$x = 9$$$.
The two auspicious 6$$$6$$$-digit numbers are codeforces gym IDs to remind us to upsolve some of our previous contests <3.
